published_title: THE STAR THAT ONLY SPOKE IN FLARES

story.title: THE STAR THAT ONLY SPOKE IN FLARES
story.deck: A ring habitat of fourteen thousand has seventy hours to decide whether its star is attacking it, and the only evidence that it is not is a silence nobody had thought to measure.
story.shape: Six scenes across four days: a council's case for flight, a physicist's nine-year ledger, a vote taken on terms the council wrote, a gap moved on purpose, a decision with a cancel line, and a night when a whole ring went quiet and the star answered in a shape no one can read yet.

scenes.title: Seventy Hours
paragraphs: *Calloway Reach, Ring Council chamber · Day 1, 07:10*

The clock on the chamber wall read 70:00:00. Someone had put it there so that it would be read aloud, and nobody had. Outside the long window the ring turned slowly under a red sun the size of a coin, with fourteen thousand people on its inner face, and the room smelled of cold tea and of a council that had not slept.

Illuminara had come aboard three weeks earlier on an ice tender, hired by the Rakel cooperative to model how heat and light loaded the cutting quays. She was in the chamber because her models were the only ones nobody had yet argued with. She stood at the back, beside the water jug.

**Teodora Vance**  
The Wick has thrown six bursts in eleven days, each one larger than the last. Each came after our evening traffic peaked, and each came in a pattern the shield office calls structured. The forecast for the seventh is one point three times the rating of our parasol. Ferries need twenty-six hours to load. The order has to go out by hour forty-two.

**Pell Rourke**  
The parasol takes one burst. I will not promise it takes that one.

**Illuminara**  
What does leaving cost?

**Teodora Vance**  
Rakel. Everything we mine. A ring that leaves carries eight months of water, and after that it's a very large cup.
Vance was sixty and square-shouldered, with the habit of putting the worst number first so that no one could accuse her of hiding it. She turned from the window to face the back of the room.

**Teodora Vance**  
Don't tell me it's talking. We have no way to know it is speaking at all, and you are asking fourteen thousand people to stay under a possible weapon on the strength of a pattern. If I'm wrong about the weapon we lose the ice and a year. If you're wrong we lose the ring.

**Illuminara**  
I won't tell you it's talking. I haven't seen enough to say so, and you would be right not to believe me if I did. I'd like your dock-clock traffic log, Dr. Brannock's flare record, and the room until the evening session.

**Teodora Vance**  
The council sits at eighteen hundred. At eighteen hundred I put the evacuation to a vote.

**Illuminara**  
Then I'll bring you something you can test before you vote.
Vance looked at the clock and then at her, and for a moment the worst-number-first habit gave way to something nearer curiosity.

**Teodora Vance**  
Test it with what? We have sixty-nine hours and fifty-one minutes.

scenes.title: Nine Years of Margins
paragraphs: *Ring observatory, Brannock's office · Day 1, 09:30*

Ilse Brannock kept the flare record in a ledger as well as on the network, because the ledger could not be edited by anyone who disliked it. Nine years of the Wick filled it, night by night, in a small upright hand with notes in the margins. Some of the notes were questions. A few were underlined twice.

**Ilse Brannock**  
You're the ice woman with the thermal models.

**Illuminara**  
Today I'm the ice woman who read your flare record. It's very clean. Who keeps it?

**Ilse Brannock**  
I do. Nobody else wanted to. A flare is a flare.

**Illuminara**  
You don't think so.
Ilse put a hand flat on the ledger as one might on a sleeping animal.

**Ilse Brannock**  
I showed this to two people. One laughed, kindly, which was worse. I said the Wick grows louder when we do. After every busy evening the next burst is larger by about the same fraction. A star's flares don't care about our trade. I knew how it sounded, so I stopped saying it.

**Illuminara**  
And the timing?

**Ilse Brannock**  
Always the small hours. I assumed the burst followed the peak and took its time. Stars are slow.

Illuminara laid the traffic log over the flare record on the glass table. The two were kept on different clocks, the observatory's on station mean time and the exchange net's on dock time, three minutes apart. Nobody had ever held both together, because the net belonged to the communications office and carried private trade.
She slid one three minutes. The bright marks on Ilse's record dropped into the troughs of the traffic like coins into a purse.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Four-oh-five. That's the shift change. The whole ring goes quiet for twenty minutes while the night crews swap.

**Illuminara**  
It isn't the loud that it answers, Doctor. It's the quiet after the loud. The louder we were, the bigger it is, and it only ever speaks when we stop.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Say what that sounds like.

**Illuminara**  
Someone raising their voice over a crowd and waiting for a gap. It is exactly the sentence that gets a woman laughed at, and I'd rather it didn't have to be mine. So tell me how I'm wrong.
Ilse took the question the way a hungry person takes bread. She stood, went to the window, and counted on her fingers without looking at them.

**Ilse Brannock**  
One. A spot group turning every twenty-four-point-one hours would fire at four-oh-five for weeks, and I'd see a ring-shaped coincidence. Two. The lull could be the effect. A flare's precursors scrub our band and the traffic drops because the star dimmed it. Three. Three nights on three instruments is three nights.

**Illuminara**  
Then we do something a habit can't do, and neither can a spinning spot or a precursor. We fill the old gap with traffic and open a new one three hours later, on purpose, and write down what each of you predicts first.

**Ilse Brannock**  
You want me at the council.

**Illuminara**  
I want the person who has listened for nine years to say what it has heard and what she isn't sure of. I'll sit behind you.

scenes.title: The Case for Flight
paragraphs: *Council chamber · Day 1, 18:00*

Vance opened the session by reading the clock aloud: fifty-nine hours, ten minutes. Then she gave the floor to Rourke, who stood with his hands behind him, like a man giving evidence in a trial he hoped to lose.

**Pell Rourke**  
Seventh burst, ordinary traffic, one point three of rating. The parasol is nine hundred metres of foil on a spine. We can edge it on to the sun and it will take more than it's built for, once. It will not be the same plate afterward, and after it comes an eighth.

**Teodora Vance**  
That's the case for flight, and I will make it myself so that nobody thinks I haven't. Evacuations fail when they start late. A star that gets louder every time we speak is a danger whether or not it means anything by it. I would rather lose the ice than argue about intent with fourteen thousand lives on the table.
Gideon Farrow rose from the guild benches before she had finished sitting. He was round and beautifully dressed and had been counting something in his head for the whole of the session.

**Gideon Farrow**  
Then I ask the other question. Who pays if we flee from a weather event? The ice is my guild's wages and the ring's drinking water. It can't be that nobody's allowed to ask whether the star is just a star.

**Teodora Vance**  
Nobody has forbidden it. Dr. Brannock?
Ilse stood. Her hands were steady on the lectern, and Illuminara, three rows back, saw her find the notes she had meant not to need.

**Ilse Brannock**  
I have nine years of flares and three nights checked on three instruments with three clocks. The timing sits in the quiet of our traffic, and the size follows the loudness before it. I have three rivals, and I can't kill them with what I have. A spot turning at twenty-four hours. A lull that is an effect rather than a cause. And plain chance.

**Teodora Vance**  
In other words you don't know.

**Ilse Brannock**  
In other words I know where I could be wrong, Chair. That's most of what I know.
Illuminara rose last and did not go to the lectern.

**Illuminara**  
I can't tell this council that the star is a mind. I can tell you that the data prefers one explanation to two others, and that there's a measurement that costs nothing and kills my explanation if I'm wrong. At four-oh-five tomorrow we fill the shift change with ordinary traffic. At seven we pause the exchange net for twenty-two minutes. If the star is a spot, it fires at four-oh-five. If the lull is its effect, our band fails then. If it is answering us, it fires in the new gap. We write the three predictions down tonight and seal them.

**Gideon Farrow**  
And what does that twenty-two minutes cost my traders?

**Illuminara**  
Tell me what they need to keep, and I'll try to leave it alone. What would you protect?

**Gideon Farrow**  
The settlement window. Nothing clears in a pause. Keep the pause off the settlement hour and I'll sell it to the guild myself.

**Illuminara**  
Seven is clear of it. Madam Chair, the cancel line is yours to write. I'll ask that it not be mine.
Vance took a pen to a sheet of paper, which was a thing nobody in the chamber had seen done in years.

**Teodora Vance**  
Any burst over nine-tenths of rating, any burst outside both windows, or any failure of the net at four-oh-five. Any one of them and the ferries load within the hour, and nobody argues with me. The manifests are cut tonight and the ferries are fuelled whatever you find. I vote at hour forty.

scenes.title: The Gap Moves
paragraphs: *Communications office, exchange net · Day 2, 06:52*

At four-oh-five the old gap had been filled, and the Wick had said nothing at all. Nadim Oyelaran told them so with a flat voice and a face that was trying not to be asked about it. The net had run at full tilt through the shift change, and the band had stayed clean, with no precursor and no scrubbing. Ilse had been awake since the previous morning and sat very straight in a chair she had not chosen.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Sealed envelope is in the council log. Three lines. Rotation says four-oh-five, which didn't happen. The effect-not-cause rival says our band fails at four-oh-five, which it didn't. Your line says seven, within twenty-five minutes either side, at between a half and seven-tenths of rating.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Say it again about the amplitude.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Last night's dusk peak was a little under average. Half to seven-tenths.

At seven the exchange net went quiet. It was not a failure and not a maintenance. It was a request, read over the ring's speakers by a Chair who did not like making requests. Kitchens went on, ferries stayed fuelled, and the trading floor went still for twenty-two minutes as fourteen thousand people agreed to stop talking over something they could not hear.
Illuminara watched the photometer on the wall. It was a flat line, then a flat line, and then it was not.

It arrived at seven-oh-two, after the old four-oh-five hour had gone by unanswered. It rose in a sharp stroke and decayed over forty minutes, with the kind of long shoulder on the descent that Ilse had marked in the margin of her ledger for nine years with a small question mark.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Fifty-eight hundredths.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
That's inside the envelope.
Nobody cheered. Ilse took off her glasses and put them down on the console, and Illuminara found, with a surprise that she let show, that she was holding the older woman's elbow.

**Ilse Brannock**  
It came late for its own clock and on time for ours.

**Illuminara**  
That's one night, Doctor. I'd like a second before anyone calls it anything.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Of course you would. So would I. Do you know, it's the first time I've wished for a second night that wasn't to catch myself out.

scenes.title: Forty Hours
paragraphs: *Council chamber · Day 2, 23:10*

The second gap had been smaller. It was eighteen minutes at half past ten, announced on the ring's speakers and in the children's nets as a quiet game, with the guild's blessing and Gideon's reluctant arithmetic. The Wick had fired at ten thirty-six, at thirty-one hundredths of rating, against a forecast of a quarter to four-tenths. Clock hour forty found the chamber very full and unnaturally silent.

**Teodora Vance**  
Two nights. Two predictions, written first, both inside their windows, neither rival close. I'll tell you what I won't say. I won't say it's a mind. I'll say that it behaves like a thing that answers our schedule, and a thing that answers our schedule can be planned around. That's a different problem from the one I was voting on at eighteen hundred yesterday.

**Pell Rourke**  
It's a problem I can work. I can edge the parasol before the burst and not after. Planned, the load falls to about a third.

**Teodora Vance**  
My objection stands, though. Suppose we speak to it and we are wrong about what we're saying. Suppose we insult it.

**Illuminara**  
We might. I can't promise we won't. What I can do is make the first thing we say the thing it has been waiting for. A quiet that we announce ourselves is the first word of an answer, before any signal. If the star hears nothing else, it hears that we stopped.

**Teodora Vance**  
And if it doesn't hear that?

**Illuminara**  
Then it fires at an hour of its own choosing, over nine-tenths, and your cancel line sends the ferries. Nothing about the line changes. You keep the right to stop me, Chair, until the last second.
Vance put her pen down. She had hold of the sheet with the cancel line on it, and she smoothed it flat, the way people do before they sign something.

**Teodora Vance**  
The ferries stay fuelled. The evacuation is cancelled, not the line. I'll put that to the council as a vote, and anyone who wants to leave on their own account may take a berth. Is there a second?

Dov Achterberg, who had spoken only once in two days, seconded it in a tone that implied he was seconding a motion to be wrong in public. It passed, nine to two. The two did not look away, and Vance did not ask them to.

Afterwards the reply was designed on a console in the communications office at one in the morning. Nadim had the ice-cutting laser, a forty-metre array that spent its life dissolving comet in the Rakel belt. Ilse had her ledger open to the long decay at the end of each flare.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
I can give it a beam. I can't tell you it'll see it.

**Illuminara**  
Neither can I. I know it listens in the band we crowd. The laser is the second line. The silence is the first.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Then nothing in it that says anything. It shouldn't speak first and it shouldn't speak long. Three pulses on the rhythm of its own rising edge, and then silence for as long as the pulses took. Heard, and your turn.

**Illuminara**  
That's the whole of it?

**Ilse Brannock**  
It's a great deal of it. I've wanted for nine years to say that much to someone who might be listening.

scenes.title: A Turn at Four-Oh-Five
paragraphs: *Calloway Reach, whole ring · Day 4, 04:05*

The largest burst was forecast for four-oh-five. Under ordinary traffic Pell Rourke's figure was one point three of rating. After the guild had agreed to cap its dusk peak by a third, which cost it the most profitable evening of the quarter, it was eight-tenths, plus or minus a seventh. The parasol stood edge-on to the sun, turned at the cost of a month's thruster propellant, and the Rakel quays had been left unshielded because there was no way to protect everything.

The ring went quiet at four-oh-one. It was the shift change, and in four minutes the night crews would hand over to the day. There was no trade on the floor, and no stream on the children's nets, and the long corridors of the inner face filled with fourteen thousand people holding still. In the communications office Nadim held the beam array a hand's breadth from firing and did not look at anyone.

**Teodora Vance**  
Any burst over nine-tenths and the line stands.

**Pell Rourke**  
Understood, Chair.
The three pulses went out at four-oh-five, and then the ring did what the star had never been given in nine years, which was to leave a space.

The flare arrived at four-oh-nine. It rose in its sharp stroke and the photometer screamed, and for forty seconds Illuminara could not make out the numbers on the wall. Then Ilse said the figure aloud, and it was seventy-four hundredths.

**Pell Rourke**  
Load on the plate is a third of that. We're holding.

They were holding. They lost two relay masts at Rakel Quay to the burst, and they would later discover that the guild had lost more trade in one evening than it earned in some months. No one was hurt. In the long decay that followed, with the beam array still silent and the ring still holding its breath, the photometer drew a shape Ilse had never seen in the whole of her ledger. It was three small steps, one after another, like someone knocking.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Three. It's three. I have nine years and it has never made three before.

**Illuminara**  
Don't read it yet. We don't know that it's a reply.

**Ilse Brannock**  
No. We don't know.

The second night they did it again, with the same quiet, the same three pulses, and a smaller burst at the right hour. The photometer drew the three steps once more, in the same places, a little smaller as the flare was.
Nobody said anything for a time. Gideon Farrow, who had come to the office to settle a bill, stood in the doorway with the bill in his hand, and did not hand it to anyone.

**Teodora Vance**  
Daily window. Forty minutes at the shift change, for as long as the council keeps voting for it, and I'll hold the cancel line myself. Dov's side won't believe a word of this, and I won't ask them to. I'll ask them to keep the silence.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Do you want to know what it said?

**Illuminara**  
I want to know whether it says it again. If it does, then perhaps one day we'll learn what it means. Until then I'm glad someone has been listening for nine years.
Ilse closed the ledger and then, after a moment, opened it again, and wrote on the next clean line with a small upright hand: *Four-oh-five. We stopped. It knocked.*

**Ilse Brannock**  
Always in a gap. I called it the small hours because that was the gap we kept giving it.

Four-oh-five. Shift change. The ring goes quiet for twenty minutes while the crews swap.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Say what you want to do.

**Illuminara**  
Move the gap. Fill four-oh-five with ordinary traffic, open a new gap at seven, and write every prediction before we touch the switches.

**Ilse Brannock**  
The exchange monitor shares the band. A precursor could fool it.

**Illuminara**  
What does not share it?

**Ilse Brannock**  
The old bolometric plate. Hard wire, separate clock, nothing in the exchange band. Rourke wanted it scrapped.

**Illuminara**  
Then it stays. And you present the test. I will not borrow nine years of your listening and call it my discovery.
Ilse looked at the double-underlined question in her ledger. *Hope is not evidence,* Illuminara thought. *But shame can hide evidence for years if nobody makes room for the person carrying it.*

**Ilse Brannock**  
I will present it if the envelope contains the ways I may be wrong.

Put them first.

scenes.title: The Case for Flight
paragraphs: *Council chamber · Day 1, 18:00*

Vance opened the session by reading the clock aloud: fifty-nine hours, ten minutes. Then she gave the floor to Rourke, who stood with his hands behind him, like a man giving evidence in a trial he hoped to lose.

**Pell Rourke**  
The dangerous dawn alignment on Day Four, ordinary traffic, one point three of rating. Our two requested test gaps may draw smaller responses before it. If they do, that is new behavior, not the seventh and eighth members of the old sequence. It may strengthen the case for turn-taking, or mean the experiment itself is increasing the hazard.

**Teodora Vance**  
That's the case for flight, and I will make it myself so nobody thinks I haven't. Evacuations fail when they start late. A star that changes because we ask it to is not automatically safer than a star that does not.
Gideon Farrow rose from the guild benches. He was round and beautifully dressed and had been counting something in his head for the whole session.

**Gideon Farrow**  
Who pays if we flee from a weather event? The ice is my guild's wages and the ring's drinking water. It can't be that nobody may ask whether the star is just a star.

**Teodora Vance**  
Nobody has forbidden it. Dr. Brannock?
Ilse stood. Her hands were steady on the lectern, and Illuminara, three rows back, saw her find the notes she had meant not to need.

**Ilse Brannock**  
I have nine years of flares, three instruments and three clocks. The timing sits in the quiet of our traffic, and the size follows the loudness before it. I have three rivals: a spot rotating every twenty-four-point-one hours, a lull caused by a precursor rather than chosen by us, and chance.

**Teodora Vance**  
How much chance?

**Ilse Brannock**  
I preserved the clustering in the nine-year record and shuffled ten thousand pairs of gaps with the same widths and traffic levels. Seven pairs caught bursts in both timing windows and both amplitude bands. Seven in ten thousand is not zero. It is also not an argument I would throw away.

**Dov Achterberg**  
A calculation built from the same ledger that suggested the question. And your windows are fifty minutes wide.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Yes. Which is why the spot and precursor predictions are sealed beside ours. If the spot fires at the old hour, we lose. If the exchange band fails while the independent plate stays quiet, we lose. If one requested result misses, we write miss before we explain anything.

**Illuminara**  
At four-oh-five tomorrow we fill the usual gap with ordinary traffic. At seven we pause the exchange net for twenty-two minutes. The independent plate remains live. We repeat with a shorter gap after the next dusk peak. The council writes the stop conditions.

**Gideon Farrow**  
What does the pause cost my traders?

**Illuminara**  
Tell the room what they need to keep.

**Gideon Farrow**  
The settlement hour. Move around it and I will sell the test to the guild. I won't sell a permanent blackout.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Nor should he. A scheduled silence is a scheduled vulnerability. Medical calls, collision alarms, smugglers who know when nobody is looking. If the proposed cure requires fourteen thousand people to become deaf on a timetable, I prefer the ferries.
Illuminara turned toward him rather than back to the lectern.

**Illuminara**  
Then the test must preserve an emergency carrier outside the crowded band, and any lasting arrangement must be movable. Nadim, can that be done without contaminating the plate?

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
A narrow red channel, hard-limited to alarms and medical speech. The plate won't see it. For a lasting window, the Chair could choose within a ninety-minute band and announce it fifteen minutes ahead.

**Teodora Vance**  
Noted. My cancel line: any requested burst over nine-tenths, any burst outside both registered windows, any failure of the independent plate, or any failure of the red channel. The ferries are fuelled tonight and manifests cut. A trigger starts loading within one hour; completing it still takes twenty-six. Nobody edits that sentence afterward.

scenes.title: The Gap Moves
paragraphs: *Communications office, exchange net · Day 2, 06:52*

At four-oh-five the old gap had been filled, and the Wick had said nothing. The exchange band stayed clean; so did the independent bolometric plate. Ilse had been awake since the previous morning and sat very straight in a chair she had not chosen.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Sealed envelope is in the council log. Rotation said four-oh-five, which did not happen. Precursor said the exchange band would fail there while the plate remained quiet, which did not happen. Turn-taking says seven, within twenty-five minutes, between half and seven-tenths of rating.

At seven the exchange net went quiet. Kitchens went on, ferries stayed fuelled, and the red emergency carrier whispered with two medical calls and one collision alarm. The trading floor stopped for twenty-two minutes as fourteen thousand people agreed to leave a space.

The hard-wired plate drew a flat line, then a flat line, and then a sharp stroke at seven-oh-two. The network monitor followed a fraction later. The long shoulder on the decay was the mark Ilse had drawn in her ledger for nine years.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Fifty-eight hundredths on the plate.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Inside timing and amplitude. Red channel never dropped.
Nobody cheered. Illuminara held Ilse's elbow only after the older woman reached for her.

**Ilse Brannock**  
One.

**Illuminara**  
One.

The second requested gap came at twenty-two thirty on the same day, after a smaller dusk peak. A weak rise appeared on the exchange monitor eleven minutes before the pause. Dov, watching from the council feed, called it a precursor. The hard-wired plate stayed level.
At twenty-two thirty-six the Wick flared. The registered amplitude band ended at forty hundredths. The plate climbed to forty-one.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Outside the envelope.

**Ilse Brannock**  
By one hundredth. It is a miss.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
The early rise was our own carrier leaking into the exchange monitor. It is absent from the plate. That defeats the precursor claim, but it does not put the amplitude back inside the envelope.

**Pell Rourke**  
And two requested responses in sixteen hours are faster than the old forty-four-hour background. If we are causing them, that matters more than whether we have taught the sun manners.
Illuminara studied the two traces and did not rescue her prediction.

**Illuminara**  
Record the timing hit, the amplitude miss, the failed precursor rival and the faster cadence. Then stop opening gaps until the council decides what the faster cadence means.

**Ilse Brannock**  
You wanted a second night.

**Illuminara**  
I wanted an answer that could tell us no. This one has.

scenes.title: Forty Hours
paragraphs: *Council chamber · Day 2, 23:10*

Clock hour forty found the chamber full. On the wall were four lines, none softened: OLD-GAP SILENCE; FIRST REQUEST HIT; SECOND REQUEST TIMING HIT / AMPLITUDE MISS; REQUESTED CADENCE FASTER THAN BACKGROUND.

**Teodora Vance**  
Nobody in this room gets to call that two clean predictions. Dr. Brannock, what survives?

**Ilse Brannock**  
The rotating-spot prediction failed at four-oh-five. The precursor prediction failed on the independent plate. In ten thousand paired shuffles, seven matched both timing and amplitude; ours matched both timings but only one amplitude. The data still prefers schedule-response. It does not prove a mind, and the faster cadence may be a cost of asking.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Then stop asking and load the ferries. The experiment changed the thing we feared.

**Pell Rourke**  
Or exposed that it was already waiting for gaps we happened to give it. The Day Four burst remains the dangerous one. With the dusk cap and the parasol turned before dawn, my median is eight-tenths. Without them, one point three.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Median. Your upper edge?

**Pell Rourke**  
Nine-tenths. At the cancel line.
The two numbers stayed between them. Vance looked not at Illuminara but at Ilse.

**Teodora Vance**  
If we stay, what do you ask the Wick to do?

**Ilse Brannock**  
Nothing beyond what the dangerous burst may do anyway. One bounded silence at dawn, three pulses from our cutter, then no second request. If the flare comes in the window and under the line, we learn whether leaving room changes the load. If not, the manifests are already cut.

**Gideon Farrow**  
The dusk cap costs the guild its best settlement of the quarter. We will take it once. Not daily, and not without the loss entered beside the science.

**Dov Achterberg**  
And no fixed daily blackout. The red channel stays open. Any later window moves inside the ninety-minute band, fifteen minutes' notice, renewed by vote each day. Security may cancel it without your permission.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
I can enforce that in hardware. Trade carrier dark; red carrier live; plate independent. Six signatures to change it.

**Illuminara**  
That is better than what I brought you.

**Teodora Vance**  
It is safer because the people paying for it changed it.
Vance kept one hand on the written cancel line.

**Teodora Vance**  
The ferries stay fuelled. Loading starts within one hour if the plate crosses nine-tenths, the flare leaves the window, the red carrier fails, or security calls the silence unsafe. Anyone may take a berth now. We attempt one bounded exchange at dawn. Dov's moving-window amendment and Farrow's cost ledger are part of the motion.
The vote passed seven to four, not nine to two. Dov voted no. His amendment passed eleven to zero.
Afterward the reply was designed in the communications office. Nadim had the forty-metre ice-cutting array. Ilse had her ledger open to the rising edge of the first requested flare.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
I can give it a beam. I can't tell you it will see it.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Three pulses on the rhythm of its own rise. Then silence for as long as the pulses took. Heard, and your turn.

**Illuminara**  
No claim about what it means.

**Ilse Brannock**  
No. Only a courtesy we can withdraw.

scenes.title: A Turn at Four-Oh-Five
paragraphs: *Calloway Reach, communications office and Rakel Quay · Day 4, 04:05*

Under ordinary traffic the dangerous burst had been forecast at one point three of parasol rating. Farrow's dusk cap cost the guild its best evening of the quarter. Turning the parasol cost a month's thruster propellant and left Rakel Quay outside its full shadow. Rourke's registered range was seven-tenths to nine-tenths. Nine-tenths remained the line.

The Chair chose four-oh-five from the ninety-minute band and announced it fifteen minutes before. The red carrier stayed live. In the communications office Nadim held the beam trigger. On Rakel Quay his sister Kemi and two riggers waited beside the relay-mast breakers, because the model said the exposed masts would take the first side-load.

**Kemi Oyelaran**  
Rakel ready. You owe me two masts if your polite sun sneezes.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Put them on Farrow's ledger.

**Gideon Farrow**  
They are already there.

At four-oh-five Nadim sent three pulses. The trade band remained silent afterward. A medical call crossed the red carrier from nursery six; a child had swallowed a button. The silence did not make the ring helpless.
Four minutes passed.
The independent plate climbed.

**Pell Rourke**  
Point six. Point seven-two. Parasol taking thirty-one percent.
A second shoulder rose under the first.

**Teodora Vance**  
Read the plate, not the model.

**Pell Rourke**  
Point eight-six.

At Rakel, the first mast began to arc. Kemi cut its breaker before the automatic relay understood what was happening. The mast folded across an empty loading rail. The second leaned toward a fuel line.

**Kemi Oyelaran**  
Losing west two. Clearing the line now.
She drove the quay tug into the mast's lower brace. Metal went down away from the fuel line, taking the tug's manipulator arm with it.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Kemi?

**Kemi Oyelaran**  
Still expensive.
The plate touched eighty-nine hundredths. For twelve seconds its uncertainty band crossed the line, though the central reading did not.

**Teodora Vance**  
Rourke.

**Pell Rourke**  
Central reading below nine. Structure stable. My recommendation is hold, Chair. Your line says over, not near.
Vance's finger rested on the loading order. She could have called uncertainty a trigger. Nobody would have blamed her.

**Teodora Vance**  
Hold. Kemi has the quay. Red carrier is live. If the central plate rises one hundredth, load.
It did not. The long shoulder fell through eight-tenths, then seven. The parasol held. Rakel lost two relay masts and one tug arm; no one was hurt.
In the decay, with Nadim's array still silent and the ring keeping the space it had promised, the independent plate drew three small steps.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Three. I have nine years and it has never made three.

**Illuminara**  
Don't read it yet. We don't know that it's a reply.

**Ilse Brannock**  
No. We know only that it happened after our three.

They did not repeat the request that night. The next day the council authorized one movable window, with the red channel and security veto intact, and required a fresh vote every seven days. Farrow entered the lost settlement, two masts, a tug arm and a month of propellant in the same ledger as the avoided evacuation. Dov signed the safety protocol and wrote beneath his name that he still believed they should leave.

**Teodora Vance**  
He is allowed to be wrong in the record, if he is wrong.

**Illuminara**  
So are we.
Ilse closed her ledger, opened it again, and wrote on the next clean line in her small upright hand: *Four-oh-five. We stopped. It knocked.*

story.title: THE STAR THAT ONLY SPOKE IN FLARES
story.deck: A ring habitat of fourteen thousand has seventy hours to decide whether its star is attacking it, and the only evidence that it is not is a silence nobody had thought to measure.
story.shape: Six scenes across four days: a council's case for flight, a physicist's nine-year ledger and the lever hidden in it, a vote taken on terms the council wrote, two moved gaps that do not answer cleanly, a decision altered by its dissenters, and a dawn when a whole ring goes quiet and the star answers in a shape no one can read yet.

scenes.title: Seventy Hours
paragraphs: *Calloway Reach, Ring Council chamber · Day 1, 06:10*

The clock on the chamber wall read 70:00:00. Someone had put it there so that it would be read aloud, and nobody had. Outside the long window the ring turned slowly under a red sun the size of a coin, with fourteen thousand people on its inner face, and the room smelled of cold tea and of a council that had not slept.

Illuminara had come aboard three weeks earlier on an ice tender, hired by the Rakel cooperative to model how heat and light loaded the cutting quays. She was in the chamber because her models were the only ones nobody had yet argued with. She stood at the back, beside the water jug.

**Teodora Vance**  
The Wick has thrown six dangerous bursts in eleven days. In nine years of records it threw about one a month. Eleven days is two hundred and sixty-four hours; six bursts in that time is one every forty-four, and that is not a fluctuation I can fold into the background. They cluster after our evening traffic peaks. The next natural alignment is due at about four in the morning on Day Four. Under ordinary traffic the shield office forecasts one point three times the rating of our parasol. Ferries need twenty-six hours to finish loading, and I will not cut a two-hour margin out of a ring's lives. The order has to go out by hour forty-two.

**Pell Rourke**  
The parasol takes one burst. I will not promise it takes that one.

**Illuminara**  
What does leaving cost?

**Teodora Vance**  
Rakel. Everything we mine. A ring that leaves carries eight months of water, and after that it's a very large cup.
Vance was sixty and square-shouldered, with the habit of putting the worst number first so that no one could accuse her of hiding it. She turned from the window to face the back of the room.

**Teodora Vance**  
Don't tell me it's talking. We have no way to know it is speaking at all, and you are asking fourteen thousand people to stay under a possible weapon on the strength of a pattern. If I'm wrong about the weapon we lose the ice and a year. If you're wrong we lose the ring.

**Illuminara**  
I won't tell you it's talking. I haven't seen enough to say so, and you would be right not to believe me if I did. I'd like your dock-clock traffic log, Dr. Brannock's flare record, the specifications of every detector, and the room until the evening session.

**Teodora Vance**  
The council sits at eighteen hundred. At eighteen hundred I put the evacuation to a vote.

**Illuminara**  
Then I'll bring you something you can test before you vote.
Vance looked at the clock and then at her. Curiosity did not soften her face; it made the responsibility in it more exact.

**Teodora Vance**  
Test it with what? We have sixty-nine hours and fifty-one minutes.

scenes.title: Nine Years of Margins
paragraphs: *Ring observatory, Brannock's office · Day 1, 09:30*

Ilse Brannock kept the flare record in a ledger as well as on the network, because the ledger could not be edited by anyone who disliked it. Nine years of the Wick filled it, night by night, in a small upright hand with questions in the margins. A few were underlined twice.

**Ilse Brannock**  
You're the ice woman with the thermal models.

**Illuminara**  
Today I'm the ice woman who read your flare record. It's very clean. Who keeps it?

**Ilse Brannock**  
I do. Nobody else wanted to. A flare is a flare.

**Illuminara**  
You don't think so.
Ilse put a hand flat on the ledger as one might on a sleeping animal.

**Ilse Brannock**  
I showed this to two people. One laughed, kindly, which was worse. I said the Wick grows louder when we do. After every busy evening the next burst is larger by about the same fraction. A star's flares don't care about our trade. I knew how it sounded, so I stopped saying it.

**Illuminara**  
And the timing?

**Ilse Brannock**  
Always in a gap. I called it the small hours because that was the gap we kept giving it.

Illuminara laid the traffic log over the flare record on the glass table. The observatory clock and dock clock were three minutes apart. Nobody had held the records together because the exchange net carried private trade.
She slid one trace by three minutes. The bright marks dropped into the troughs of the traffic like coins into a purse.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Four-oh-five. Shift change. The ring goes quiet for twenty minutes while the crews swap.

**Illuminara**  
The size follows the loudness before the gap. The timing follows the gap itself. If there is an intention here, the least extravagant account is not anger. It is turn-taking: something raising its voice over a crowd, then waiting not to be overwritten. But the same trace could still come from a rotating spot, a precursor that suppresses our band, or chance.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Say what you want to do.

**Illuminara**  
Move the gap. Fill four-oh-five with ordinary traffic, open a new gap at seven, and write every prediction before we touch the switches.

**Ilse Brannock**  
The exchange monitor shares the band. A precursor could fool it.

**Illuminara**  
What does not share it?

**Ilse Brannock**  
The old bolometric plate. Hard wire, separate clock, nothing in the exchange band. Rourke wanted it scrapped.

**Illuminara**  
Then it stays. And you present the test. I will not borrow nine years of your listening and call it my discovery.
Ilse looked at the double-underlined question in her ledger. *Hope is not evidence,* Illuminara thought. *But shame can hide evidence for years if nobody makes room for the person carrying it.*

Illuminara turned the ledger's pages back to the worst flares and forward to the Day Four forecast, and stopped. The test would tell them whether the star kept time. It would not shrink the burst already coming.

**Illuminara**  
One more thing, and it is a question about your own margins. If the size follows the loudness before the gap, then the Day Four burst is not fixed. It is being sized right now by what we do on the evening of Day Three. What happens to the flare after a quiet evening?

Ilse turned eight pages without looking for them. The smallest flares in the book were all there: the nights after the ring had gone dark for the harvest festival, when the trade band was nearly empty by dusk.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Small. They're the smallest in the book. I put them down to the calendar.

**Illuminara**  
Then the lever is the dusk peak, not the gap. If the council can cap one evening's traffic before the Day Four alignment, the parasol may meet something near eight-tenths instead of one point three. Pell will have to model it. I can't promise it. I can tell you which number to try to move.

**Ilse Brannock**  
I will present it if the envelope contains the ways I may be wrong.

**Illuminara**  
Put them first.

scenes.title: The Case for Flight
paragraphs: *Council chamber · Day 1, 18:00*

Vance opened the session by reading the clock aloud: fifty-eight hours, ten minutes. Then she gave the floor to Rourke, who stood with his hands behind him, like a man giving evidence in a trial he hoped to lose.

**Pell Rourke**  
The dangerous dawn alignment on Day Four, ordinary traffic, one point three of rating. Our two requested test gaps may draw smaller responses before it. If they do, that is new behavior, not the seventh and eighth members of the old sequence. It may strengthen the case for turn-taking, or mean the experiment itself is increasing the hazard.

**Teodora Vance**  
That's the case for flight, and I will make it myself so nobody thinks I haven't. Evacuations fail when they start late. A star that changes because we ask it to is not automatically safer than a star that does not.
Gideon Farrow rose from the guild benches. He was round and beautifully dressed and had been counting something in his head for the whole session.

**Gideon Farrow**  
Who pays if we flee from a weather event? The ice is my guild's wages and the ring's drinking water. It can't be that nobody may ask whether the star is just a star.

**Teodora Vance**  
Nobody has forbidden it. Dr. Brannock?
Ilse stood. Her hands were steady on the lectern, and Illuminara, three rows back, saw her find the notes she had meant not to need.

**Ilse Brannock**  
I have nine years of flares, three instruments and three clocks. The timing sits in the quiet of our traffic, and the size follows the loudness before it. I have three rivals: a spot rotating every twenty-four-point-one hours, a lull caused by a precursor rather than chosen by us, and chance.

**Teodora Vance**  
How much chance?

**Ilse Brannock**  
I kept the clustering and the one-a-month background of the nine-year record, and shuffled ten thousand pairs of gaps with the same widths and traffic levels. Seven pairs caught bursts in both timing windows and both amplitude bands. Seven in ten thousand is not zero. It is also not an argument I would throw away.

**Dov Achterberg**  
A calculation built from the same ledger that suggested the question. And your windows are fifty minutes wide.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Yes. Which is why the spot and precursor predictions are sealed beside ours. If the spot fires at the old hour, we lose. If the exchange band fails while the independent plate stays quiet, we lose. If one requested result misses, we write miss before we explain anything.

**Illuminara**  
At four-oh-five tomorrow we fill the usual gap with ordinary traffic. At seven we pause the exchange net for twenty-two minutes. The independent plate remains live. We repeat with a shorter gap after the next dusk peak. And there is a second lever, which the ledger itself points to. The size follows the loudness before the gap, so the Day Four burst is being sized by the evening of Day Three. If the guild caps that one dusk peak, Pell's median should fall well below the parasol's rating. That is a prediction too, and it can fail. The council writes the stop conditions.

**Gideon Farrow**  
What does the pause cost my traders? And what does your cap cost them?

**Illuminara**  
Tell the room what they need to keep.

**Gideon Farrow**  
The settlement hour. Move around it and I will sell the test to the guild. The cap I will price tonight, and the number will not be small: that dusk is my best evening of the quarter. I won't sell a permanent blackout, and I won't sell a permanent cap.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Nor should he. A scheduled silence is a scheduled vulnerability. Medical calls, collision alarms, smugglers who know when nobody is looking. If the proposed cure requires fourteen thousand people to become deaf on a timetable, I prefer the ferries.
Illuminara turned toward him rather than back to the lectern.

**Illuminara**  
Then the test must preserve an emergency carrier outside the crowded band, and any lasting arrangement must be movable. Nadim, can that be done without contaminating the plate?

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
A narrow red channel, hard-limited to alarms and medical speech. The plate won't see it. For a lasting window, the Chair could choose within a ninety-minute band and announce it fifteen minutes ahead.

**Teodora Vance**  
Noted. My cancel line: any requested burst over nine-tenths, any burst outside both registered windows, any failure of the independent plate, or any failure of the red channel. The ferries are fuelled tonight and manifests cut. A trigger starts loading within one hour; completing it still takes twenty-six. Nobody edits that sentence afterward.

scenes.title: The Gap Moves
paragraphs: *Communications office, exchange net · Day 2, 06:52*

At four-oh-five the old gap had been filled, and the Wick had said nothing. The exchange band stayed clean; so did the independent bolometric plate. Ilse had been awake since the previous morning and sat very straight in a chair she had not chosen.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Sealed envelope is in the council log. Rotation said four-oh-five, which did not happen. Precursor said the exchange band would fail there while the plate remained quiet, which did not happen. Turn-taking says seven, within twenty-five minutes, between half and seven-tenths of rating.

The pause had been posted in the council log the evening before, so that every office would know to expect it. At seven the exchange net went quiet. Kitchens went on, ferries stayed fuelled, and the red emergency carrier whispered with two medical calls and one collision alarm. The trading floor stopped for twenty-two minutes as fourteen thousand people agreed to leave a space.

The hard-wired plate drew a flat line, then a flat line, and then a sharp stroke at seven-oh-two. The network monitor followed a fraction later. The long shoulder on the decay was the mark Ilse had drawn in her ledger for nine years.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Fifty-eight hundredths on the plate.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
Inside timing and amplitude. Red channel never dropped.
Nobody cheered. Illuminara held Ilse's elbow only after the older woman reached for her.

**Ilse Brannock**  
One.

**Illuminara**  
One.

At seven-oh-six a cargo tug on the outer rail killed its transponder and began drifting toward the customs lock. Dov's security desk saw it only because the lock's alarm line rode the red carrier, and the desk had four minutes to seal the lock before the tug's crew reached it.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Lock six sealed. Tug has gone back to its berth. They knew our hour because we posted our hour.
He said it to the room, not to Illuminara, and he did not say *I told you.* The tug's name went into the log beside the minutes.

The second requested gap came at twenty-two thirty on the same day, after a smaller dusk peak than the evening before: a stalled ferry queue the guild had not planned. A weak rise appeared on the exchange monitor eleven minutes before the pause. Dov, watching from the council feed, called it a precursor. The hard-wired plate stayed level.
At twenty-two thirty-six the Wick flared. The registered amplitude band ended at forty hundredths. The plate climbed to forty-one.

**Dov Achterberg**  
Outside the envelope.

**Ilse Brannock**  
By one hundredth. It is a miss.

**Nadim Oyelaran**  
The early rise was our own carrier leaking into the exchange monitor. It is absent from the plate. That defeats the precursor claim, but it does not put the amplitude back inside the envelope.

**Pell Rourke**  
And two requested responses in sixteen hours are faster than even the forty-four-hour cluster we started with. If we are causing them, that matters more than whether we have taught the sun manners.

Illuminara studied the two traces and did not rescue her prediction. Beside the second trace Ilse had written the evening's peak, and beside the first, the evening before. She set the two numbers side by side and left them without comment.

**Ilse Brannock**  
Fifty-eight hundredths after the loud evening. Forty-one after the quiet one.

**Pell Rourke**  
One pair.

**Ilse Brannock**  
One pair. It fell the right way. It is not a law, and I will not write it as one.

**Illuminara**  
Record the timing hit, the amplitude miss, the failed precursor rival, the faster cadence and the pair of evenings. Then stop opening gaps until the council decides what the faster cadence means.

**Ilse Brannock**  
You wanted a second night.

**Illuminara**  
I wanted an answer that could tell us no. This one has.

**Pell Rourke**

They did not repeat the request that night. The next day the council authorized one movable window, with the red channel and security veto intact, and required a fresh vote every seven days. Dov's desk added a standing check of the outer rail to every window, a duty the protocol still carries under his name. Farrow entered the lost settlement, two masts, a tug arm and a month of propellant in the same ledger as the avoided evacuation. Dov signed the safety protocol and wrote beneath his name that he still believed they should leave.

**Teodora Vance**  
He is allowed to be wrong in the record, if he is wrong.

**Illuminara**  
So are we.
Ilse closed her ledger, opened it again, and wrote on the next clean line in her small upright hand: *Four-oh-five. We stopped. It knocked.*
